title: Karmic tail 21-4-10 in the destiny matrix: the oppressed soul, a chain of roses and a wheel that cannot be stopped

seo.title: Karmic tail 21-4-10 in the destiny matrix: “The Oppressed Soul”
seo.description: 21-4-10 is called “The Oppressed Soul”. Why this tail's cage is made of roses and gold, what the prisoner Boethius knew about it, and where the way out is.

short: The karmic tail 21-4-10 is The World at the entry, The Emperor as the mechanism and The Wheel of Fortune at the root, and everyone who has it also has Strength at the centre of the chart. The tail has one scenario: a person reaches for a whole world, walls it in to keep it safe and ends up inside their own fortress, while the wheel turns anyway and brings them back to the start. The tail's folk name is "The Oppressed Soul". The weight here is rarely made of iron. More often it is made of the things a person values most: order, protection and permanence.

paragraphs: In Russian-speaking destiny matrix circles the tail has two closely related folk names: "The Oppressed Soul" (Ugnetyonnaya dusha) and "The Oppressed Spirit" (Ugnetyonny dukh). The legends behind them disagree on the main point: who oppressed whom. In one version the soul spent its past life under someone else's will — in subordination, in a rigid hierarchy, with no right to decide for itself — and got used to giving up its own wishes. In the other it was that will: it laid down strict rules, demanded that everyone fit them and broke whatever did not fit. The legends agree on the conclusion: now decisions, change and freedom — one's own or other people's — come hard.

There is no way to verify the legend. Numbers say nothing about past lives, and the tarot books behind the meanings of the arcana know nothing of the destiny matrix or of karmic tails. But the name does not rest on the legend alone. It can be read in the word itself and in the cards themselves.

The Russian verb ugnetat, "to oppress", comes from gnesti, "to press down". A gnyot in an old household is the weight placed on top of a barrel of pickled cabbage to press it down. The oppressed is the one with a gnyot on top. And Arthur Edward Waite, the author of the classic tarot deck and of the key book that goes with it, would have had a detailed commentary on that word: in his descriptions of the tail's cards and of its centre card, again and again the talk is of a weight a person carries, and of chains. Only these chains are not made of iron.

sections.h2: A chain of roses: the evidence in the cards themselves
paragraphs: Writing about the history of The World's image, Waite notes that the garland around the dancing figure looks "as if it were a chain of flowers intended to symbolize all sensible things." He then gives the view of the French occultist Paul Christian that the garland should be made of roses, and adds that "this is the kind of chain which Éliphas Lévi says is **less easily broken than a chain of iron**." The next sentence reads almost like a parable: "Perhaps by antithesis, but for the same reason, the iron crown of Peter may lie more lightly on the heads of sovereign pontiffs than the crown of gold on kings."

One paragraph about the tail's first card holds its two main clues. A chain of roses holds tighter than an iron one. A crown of gold weighs more than an iron one. And a crowned monarch — that is how Waite describes The Emperor — is the tail's second card.

The centre card carries the same theme on. Everyone with 21-4-10 has Strength there, and it has the same chain. The woman on Waite's card has already tamed the lion, "which is being led by a chain of flowers." The chain of flowers, Waite explains, signifies among other things "the sweet yoke and the light burden of Divine Law, when it has been taken into the heart of hearts." It is a clear echo of the Gospel: "For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light."

The root completes the picture. Benebell Wen, author of the modern textbook Holistic Tarot, opens her description of the Wheel with the words: **"Key 10: Wheel of Fortune is the karma card."** The card, she writes, can be "a foreshadowing that history will repeat itself": the past will become the future, down to a sense of déjà vu.

The legend tells this tail roughly; the cards tell it precisely. At the entry there is open space wrapped in a chain of roses. In the mechanism there is a king in a heavy golden crown. At the root there is a wheel that repeats history. At the centre there is the same chain of flowers, only worn by choice. The 21-4-10 tail is not about a person being put in chains. It is about how the most precious things — open space, order, security — become a weight on top, and about the condition under which that same chain stops being one.

sections.h2: The World at the entry: the best card in the deck at the door of the loop
paragraphs: The tail's first card sits at point M, where the scenario starts. It is the first reaction at the moment a situation becomes truly personal. In 21-4-10 that reaction is a pull towards the whole. Not towards one step, but straight towards the world: to see everything, take in everything, finish everything so that nothing is left undone.

Wen writes that The World "is considered the best card in the tarot deck": fulfilment, completion, "the Seeker's oneness with his or her greater calling." It is "the card of synthesis", holding all four elements. Waite sees in it "the perfection and end of the Cosmos" and, on the earthly level, "the swirl of the sensitive life, of joy attained in the body, of the soul's intoxication in the earthly paradise." The happiest card in the deck stands at the door of a karmic loop, and that is the tail's first oddity.

The second oddity shows in Waite's divinatory lists. The World upright: "Assured success, recompense, voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place." Reversed: "Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence." A calculated number cannot land upside down, so both lists belong to the same card, and the tail's entry holds both halves at once. The urge to break loose and the ability to freeze for years are two answers of one soul to one question: where is my open space?

Wen adds a detail that sounds especially pointed for a karmic tail. If The World appears in the position of the past, she writes, "it suggests the state that is predetermined or outlined for the Seeker, though whether the Seeker will walk the path of manifesting that full potential is to be determined by present conditions and choices." The entry of 21-4-10 is exactly such a sketch of a whole world. It is promised, not handed over.

Point M has one more property: it opens two routes at once — the karmic tail M → N → D and the relationship line M → R1 → R. So everyone with 21-4-10 also has The World at the start of the relationship line. A partner easily becomes a whole world to them. And then the mechanism takes over.

sections.h2: The Emperor as the mechanism: an orb is a thing that is held
paragraphs: The second card sits at point N, in the mechanism that keeps the repetition going even after a person has understood everything about themselves. Here stands The Emperor.

Waite describes him briefly: sceptre, crown, a throne fronted by rams' heads and **"a globe in his left hand"**. In Russian this emblem of rule is called a derzhava, from derzhat, "to hold". The world that was open space at the entry ends up in a hand in the mechanism: it is taken, put in order and held. Wen says the same in the language of power: "the orb is his dominion", "All is in order, under control."

There is nothing wrong with this in itself. Waite's divinatory list for The Emperor begins with "Stability, power, protection, realization" and ends with "also authority and will." The Emperor builds walls, and walls protect. The trouble is that walls cannot tell what they are protecting against — a storm or open space. Order set up for safety becomes a routine that must not be broken. A house built for living becomes a fortress that cannot be left. "It's safer this way" turns into "there is no other way".

Behind The Emperor, Wen sees a parched kingdom — "dry, jagged rocks" and "a small stream" at their foot — and reads in it "a thirst for a different kind of sovereignty than the one the Seeker has attained." The golden orb in his hand reminds her of King Midas, who "died of hunger, because all that he touched turned to gold and **gold cannot nourish**." "More tragic yet," she writes, "the king turned his beloved daughter to gold." This is an exact image of the 21-4-10 mechanism. Everything alive that comes in through the entry — love, work, a city, a dream — the mechanism turns into a treasure to be kept. And what is kept stops moving. Gold does not spoil, but it does not grow either.

The Russian language holds both halves of this mechanism in one word. Volya is the power to command: The Emperor's "authority and will". And volya is also freedom: to go out na volyu, "to freedom", or to languish in nevolya, "captivity". Pushkin wrote: "There is no happiness on earth, but there is peace and volya" — and two lines later: "Long since, a weary slave, I have been plotting my escape." In 21-4-10 one volya builds walls while the other asks to be let out, and both belong to the same person.

That is why each legend about the tail is half right. The oppressed and the oppressor here do not live in different lives; they sit in different seats of one mechanism. A person can live under someone else's throne — a strict parent, a domineering partner, a system with rigid rules — and feel protected. A person can take the throne and keep everyone around in order. Or a person can be both on the throne and under it at once, governing themselves more harshly than any outsider would. Waite left a caveat on this card: The Emperor's rule is "the lordship of thought rather than of the animal world", and "theirs is not consciously the wisdom which draws from a higher world." A mind that builds walls does not know why a living thing needs open space.

sections.h2: The Wheel of Fortune at the root: the karma card and a sphinx amid motion
paragraphs: The third card sits at point D, the root to which the whole chain returns. Here stands The Wheel of Fortune, and it is hard to imagine a more fitting root for a karmic tail. "The karma card," in Wen's words. "What goes up will come down. What hits bottom will bounce up." History repeats, the past becomes the future. Wen also brings in samsara, "the Buddhist and Hindu concept of the endless cycle of birth and death", which "can only be ended by divine knowledge or spiritual ascension."

Here the tail meets its main conflict. The Emperor in the mechanism wants stability. The Wheel at the root does not stop. Every time the walls are finished, the wheel turns: circumstances, people, age and times change. What was built stops fitting. A person either holds the fortress to the last or flees it — and builds the same one in a new place. The loop closes.

Waite hid the key to this conflict in one sentence about the sphinx. The sphinx on the wheel, he writes, "is the equilibrium therein." "Sometimes the sphinx is represented couchant on a pedestal above, which **defrauds the symbolism** by stultifying the essential idea of stability amidst movement." The 21-4-10 mechanism does exactly what Waite objected to: it takes the sphinx off the wheel and puts it on a pedestal. It looks for stability outside motion — in walls, rules, sameness. The symbol holds no such stability.

A second sentence of Waite's answers the fatalism that can explain any loop: "that's how it worked out", "it's fate". "Behind the general notion expressed in the symbol," he writes, "there lies the denial of chance and the fatality which is implied therein." The Wheel at the root is neither a sentence nor a lottery. It is a task: to learn to stand on something that turns.

Even Waite's divinatory list for this card argues with the familiar fear. Upright: "Destiny, fortune, success, elevation, luck, felicity." Reversed: not "bad luck", as many write, but "Increase, abundance, superfluity." The Wheel does not punish. Its turn includes both the way down and the way up, and one cannot be stopped without stopping the other.

The root also echoes the entry, quietly. In the angles of the Wheel, Waite places the four Living Creatures of Ezekiel — and the same four creatures surround The World's garland. The tail begins and ends under the same guard, and between them stands The Emperor, arcanum number four.
The tail's root task, in our reading, is **not walls against change, but a centre that holds while everything moves**. Where that centre is, the chart says plainly.

sections.h2: The hidden fourth card: everyone with 21-4-10 has Strength at the centre
paragraphs: The tail has a card that is not part of the triple itself, yet everyone who has the tail has it. At the centre of the matrix, the point called the comfort zone, everyone with 21-4-10 has Strength, arcanum 11. That is how the arithmetic works: the entry point is the sum of the root and the centre, and The World (21) comes out of The Wheel (10) only together with Strength (11). No other number can stand at the centre with this tail.

This sum is the tail's most interesting equation: **The Wheel plus Strength make The World**. The open space a person reaches for at the entry is not made of walls. It is made of a turning that cannot be stopped and a strength that has no need to press down. Wen comes at this from another side: in the progression of the Major Arcana, she writes, "Strength is a foreshadowing of what it will take for a Seeker to reach Judgement and The World."

Waite's Strength is a woman closing a lion's jaws. "Her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion," and it is led by a chain of flowers. The same chain winds around The World. The difference is not in the chain but in how it was put on. Strength's chain is a law taken into the heart of hearts, not one fastened from outside. Waite insists that "the card has nothing to do with self-confidence in the ordinary sense": "she who is called Strength is the higher nature in its liberation."

Wen draws the line between two kinds of strength most clearly. The Chariot is "strength to master the world". Strength is "strength to master the self". This card, she writes, "is about domination over the Seeker's fears", a reminder that "the Seeker cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; the Seeker must use gentle, subtle influence." This is a direct reply to The Emperor in the mechanism. The stability he looks for in walls and control lies at the centre of the chart: in mastery over one's own lion, that is, over the fear of change.

There is a warning too. Waite's reversed list for Strength begins with "Despotism, abuse of power". Strength and The Emperor share a shadow: when gentle mastery of oneself is replaced by hard control over everyone, the centre of the chart turns into one more throne.

One more point is the same for everyone with the tail — Manipura, the chakra of will and status: 11-11-22, two Strengths and The Fool. Waite's Fool pauses at the edge of a precipice, "with light step, as if earth and its trammels had little power to restrain him." A tail called "The Oppressed Soul" has, in the chakra of will, the card of someone whom fetters do not hold. This link is ours, not a statement from the books. But it shows where the centre leads: not to escaping the chains, but to a lightness in which they stop holding.

sections.h2: How the 21-4-10 loop turns: open space, orb, weight, turn
paragraphs: Put the four cards into one movement, and the result is a loop of five steps. The setting differs for everyone; the moves are the same.

ol: **Open space.** Something becomes a whole world: a person, a job, a city, an idea. The entry brings a sense of fullness and freedom.
**The orb.** So as not to lose it, the world is taken in hand: routine, rules, control, "let's make it safe". It works — for a while.
**The weight.** The order sets hard. Protection becomes walls, security becomes permanence, the living becomes gold. A feeling creeps in that life is happening somewhere outside.
**The turn.** The Wheel moves anyway. The walls crack under change, or the person breaks them down and runs.
**A new orb.** In a new place, with a new person, in a new job, the world is taken in hand again. The past becomes the future.

paragraphs: People usually look for the way out at the fourth step — in escape. But escape only moves the walls to a new place. The real fork, in our reading, lies between the second and third steps: where order can still be taken into the heart, like Strength's chain, rather than strapped on as a weight.

sections.h2: The prisoner and the Wheel of Fortune: a book written from inside the loop
paragraphs: The Romans already knew the image of Fortune's wheel, but it was a book written in prison that made it one of the great images of the Middle Ages. And much of that book reads like a study of the 21-4-10 tail.

Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius was born around 480 in Rome, into one of its noblest families. He translated Aristotle, wrote on music and arithmetic, and became consul in 510. In 522 he reached the top: Theodoric, the Ostrogothic king who ruled Italy, made him magister officiorum, head of the court administration, and his two young sons were made consuls in the same year. Within a year Boethius defended the senator Albinus, who was accused of treasonous letters to the emperor in Constantinople — and was accused himself. He was imprisoned in Pavia and executed in 524.

In prison he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy. Philosophy, in the form of a woman of great dignity, appears to the prisoner as he mourns what he has lost, and their conversation became one of the most widely read books of the Middle Ages.
First Philosophy strikes at the mechanism itself: "Are you really trying to hold back the rush of a turning wheel? Most foolish of mortals, if it stops, it is no longer Fortune."

Then she gives the floor to Fortune herself. Fortune says: "This is my power, this is the game I play without end: I turn the wheel, and I delight in bringing the high down and raising the low. Climb up if you like — but on one condition: do not call it a wrong when the rules of my game require you to come down." She refuses permanence: shall the insatiable greed of men bind her to a constancy foreign to her nature? Waite's reversed World is "permanence". Boethius's Fortune is its denial. And she ends with advice: having been placed in a kingdom common to all, do not wish to live by a law of your own. One sentence holds The World, a kingdom common to all, and The Emperor, a law of one's own.

Centuries later the wheel from this book was being drawn in manuscripts. In a thirteenth-century collection known as Carmina Burana, four figures around the wheel are labelled "I shall reign", "I reign", "I have reigned", "I am without a kingdom". At the top sits a crowned king; at the bottom, the one who has lost power. The medieval Wheel of Fortune is in effect The Emperor seated on The Wheel: the mechanism and the root of the 21-4-10 tail in one picture.

Already in the first book Philosophy has words for the prisoner that strike deeper than reproach. He thinks of himself as an exile, and she tells him that he has not been driven from his homeland but has strayed from it — and if he prefers to call it exile, then he has rather exiled himself: no one else would ever have had the right to do it. In that homeland, she adds, there is one king, and to be guided by his reins and to obey his justice **is freedom itself**. A rule obeyed as freedom is the same chain of flowers that Strength wears.

In one of the book's poems Boethius writes of lions that wear beautiful chains and take food from the hand until they taste blood, and of a songbird in a cage. People take care to bring it cups smeared with honey and plenty of food. But if, hopping about its narrow cage, it catches sight of the shade of the woods, it tramples the scattered treats and longs only for the forest. This may be the most exact description of the 21-4-10 entry locked in by the mechanism: the cage is caring, the food is honeyed, and the bird can see the forest.

The most important thing Philosophy says comes in the fourth book, and it is almost a diagram of the matrix with its centre. Several circles turn around one centre. The innermost is closest to the simplicity of the middle and itself serves as a pivot for the rest; the outermost sweeps around the widest circle. "So too whatever departs farther from the first mind is caught more deeply in the nets of fate," Boethius writes, "and each thing is the freer from fate the nearer it comes to that pivot of all things." The farther from the centre, the harder the wheel spins. The nearer the centre, the freer. Everyone with 21-4-10 has Strength at the centre of the chart.

And in the fifth book Boethius finds a phrase that could serve as an epigraph to the whole tail. Souls, he writes, are freest when they contemplate what is highest, and grow less free as they sink towards the earthly. By giving in to harmful passions and consenting to them, they help along the slavery they have brought on themselves, and become **"in a way, captives of their own freedom."**

An honest caveat: no one knows Boethius's date of birth, so his tail cannot be calculated. His story proves nothing about people with 21-4-10, and the comparison with the cards is ours. But it shows what this loop looks like when it is walked all the way through: from the height of power, through prison, to the centre where the wheel no longer spins.

There is a Russian version of the same loop, one that every Russian schoolchild reads. Lermontov's Mtsyri is a mountain boy carried off as a captive by a Russian general. The sick child is left at a monastery, and a monk nurses him back to life "within protecting walls". The captivity here is not a prison but a caring one — the very chain of roses. "But in time he grew used to captivity," Lermontov writes.

And yet the young man runs away and for three days sees the world: "Hills crowned with a wreath / Of trees grown wide all round, / Rustling like a fresh crowd, / Like brothers in a round dance." And then: "But in vain I argued with fate: / It laughed at me!" The runaway comes out of the forest, looks around and recognises the place: "...for a long time / I could not grasp that once again / I had come back to my prison." The escape had traced a circle. A fictional hero has no date of birth and no tail. But "I lived but little, and lived in captivity" may be the shortest formula for "The Oppressed Soul" in Russian literature.
The loop is recognised not by events but by its moves: open space, walls, a turn, new walls. Below are typical settings. The tail does not predict which of them will come up; it describes the moves.

paragraphs.h3: In a couple: behind a stone wall

paragraphs: At first a partner becomes a whole world: with them a person wants everything at once — the road, plans, a shared future. Then the mechanism gets to work. Shared life gathers rules, the budget becomes a spreadsheet, weekends become a schedule. Some people with this tail build the fortress themselves and honestly do not understand why their partner feels cramped in it. Others choose someone who will build it: in Russian, "with him it's like being behind a stone wall". The saying is honest: a stone wall both protects and locks in.

When it gets cramped, the wheel turns: "I need air", coldness, leaving. And in the next relationship the same order repeats, only with a different face. Sometimes it is not the person with the tail who feels cramped but their partner, and then the loop runs the other way: the one who built the walls is suddenly left alone in an empty fortress.

On family matters the tail speaks in the voice of caring order: routine, rules, "we know better what is good for you". Here order is felt as protection and as a weight at the same time, and gratitude for the walls mixes with longing for open space.

After that the paths split. Some carefully carry their parents' walls inside them and live by rules whose purpose no one remembers. Others build the same walls for their own children, "so that everything is safe". Still others spend years fighting any authority at all. Wen names one side of The Emperor reversed as "the overthrow of authority or an authoritarian figure" and sums it up: "The Emperor in reverse is about dominating the domineering." But revolt against the throne is still life in the throne room: all the attention still belongs to the throne.

paragraphs.h3: In work and money: golden handcuffs

paragraphs: A job that was once a whole world becomes stability, and stability becomes a place that cannot be left: salary, mortgage, deferred bonuses, "two more years and then". Business English has an exact phrase for it — golden handcuffs. The reverse version: a person leaves the system for the sake of freedom, starts their own business and a few years later finds they have built a stricter system than the old one, where everything rests on their control and a holiday is impossible.

The Wheel at the root makes money itself a theme. Downturns and upturns are felt not as the turning of the wheel but as a threat to the fortress, and every turn is answered with a new wall: savings beyond any need, control over every expense, refusal of any risk.

paragraphs.h3: Inside: a suitcase packed in the head

paragraphs: The quietest form is an inner dialogue between open space and walls. A suitcase has long been packed in the head: move to the sea, change profession, start over. Next to it lies an equally solid list of reasons why not now. The World at the entry wants everything to be whole and complete, so starting is frightening: what if it does not come out perfect?

Wen describes The World reversed in almost these words: the Seeker "is afraid of change and is hesitating to take the necessary actions", while "triumph and supreme greatness will come, but are delayed." From the outside this looks like constancy. From the inside it feels like life in a waiting room.

sections.h2: The price: what a golden cage costs
paragraphs: The first price is a deferred life. Everything important is put off until "later": when the mortgage is paid, when the children grow up, when things are in order. The World at the entry promises fullness, the mechanism saves it up, and the savings are never spent.

The second is gold that does not nourish. There is stability, the fortress stands, but there is no joy. Wen sees a parched kingdom behind The Emperor and "a thirst for a different kind of sovereignty than the one the Seeker has attained." A well-ordered life with no air in it is an exact description of that.

The third is a cage for others. Someone who keeps themselves in order sooner or later starts keeping their loved ones in order too: deciding for them, checking on them, shielding them from life. Both books warn about this: Waite's reversed Strength begins with "Despotism, abuse of power", and for The Emperor reversed Wen writes of "a harshness and bias to the Seeker's leadership."

The fourth is running in circles. Moves, break-ups, job changes, after which everything falls into the same shape again. Boethius described this best of all: the outer circle sweeps wider than the rest and is also the farthest from the centre.

The fifth is fatalism. "It's fate", "that's how the wheel turned". It is the most convenient explanation of the loop and the one the card supports least: Waite sees in the Wheel a denial of fatality, not proof of it.

If the sense of being trapped becomes unbearable, gets in the way of sleep and daily life, or turns to thoughts of self-harm, that is a reason to contact a psychologist or counsellor straight away, and in danger to call your local emergency number or a local crisis line. And separately: if the pressure comes from another person — threats, surveillance, money taken away, bans on seeing people, violence — this is not a karmic scenario to work through but a situation that calls for help: your local emergency number and crisis services. Reading the tail is a language for watching oneself, not an explanation of someone else's cruelty.

sections.h2: Support or cage: how to tell them apart
paragraphs: Order matters for 21-4-10: The Emperor in the mechanism is not a mistake but a resource. The question is what that order has become — Strength's chain or a weight on top. A few signs show the difference.

head: Sign
Support: Strength's chain
Cage: a weight on top
rows: chosen, and its purpose is clear
"it has to be", "it's always been this way"
it is held to the last
the peace of mind of the one holding it
the door is open: leaving and coming back are both possible

sections.h2: How to leave the loop: eight practices
paragraphs: The tail cannot be cancelled, and there is no "bad card" to pull out of it: The World, The Emperor and The Wheel are resources in themselves. The task is to give each card its proper place: to The World, open space that is lived and not just kept; to The Emperor, order that serves what is alive; to The Wheel, motion that has a centre.

ol: **Audit the walls.** Write down the rules life runs on: routines, bans on oneself, compulsory "musts". Ask of each one what it protects and who set it. Keep the load-bearing walls and take down the rest. Order that has an answer to "why" holds like Strength's chain; order without one is a weight on top.

**A review date for every rule.** Make big decisions about order — the budget, the routine, agreements in a couple — together with a date for reviewing them. An Emperor who knows the council will meet again in six months does not turn a wall into a fortress.

**Small doses of open space, regularly.** Instead of one big escape every few years, small outings every week: a new route, a day without a plan, a trip somewhere new. Waite's World is both "route" and "change of place"; given a little at a time, the urge to flee does not build up.

**Find the sphinx.** When change begins, do not ask "how do I stop this" but "what in me stays steady while everything moves". Values, close people, a craft, a routine for the body — these are the axle of the wheel. Stability amid motion, not instead of it.

**Build together, not for someone else.** In a couple and in a family, before putting things in order, ask what kind of order the other person needs. Offer support, not walls. Protecting is not the same as deciding for someone.

**Finish at "good enough".** The World is the card of completion, and its shadow is waiting for perfect fullness. Close cycles when the job is done well, not flawlessly: unfinished business holds tighter than any wall.

**Work with the lion, not with the world.** When the urge comes to control everything, name the fear behind it and take one small action with that fear. Strength, for Wen, is mastery over one's own fears, not over circumstances and people.

**Separate the burden from the weight.** Once a month, go through what is being carried: obligations, roles, debts, habits. What was chosen and taken into the heart is a burden, and it can be carried lightly. What lies on top without consent is a weight: it should be taken off or chosen again, this time freely.

paragraphs: A sign that the loop has loosened: **staying no longer means "giving in", and leaving no longer means "running away"**. Order can be changed without tearing the house down, and the door of the house opens both ways.

sections.h2: The strong version of 21-4-10: a dance inside the garland
paragraphs: The strong version of the tail is a person who knows both open space and walls and can hold them together. They do not mistake freedom for the absence of limits. Waite's World figure dances inside the garland: it is "joy attained in the body", yet "still guarded by the Divine Watchers". A dance inside the frame, not an escape from it.

Such people are good at building things that others are free inside: families where the rules are explained, teams where order serves the work, workshops, schools, communities. They can be trusted with a system: they know its cost from the inside and will not let it become a cage. The Emperor gives them a rare ability to bring an idea into form, The World a sense of the whole, The Wheel the understanding that every form is temporary.

And they can stand on a turning wheel. Change does not knock them out of the saddle, because their stability lies not in walls but at the centre, where everyone with the tail has Strength. Boethius would have called it a freedom that grows the nearer one comes to the pivot. The Gospel would have called it a yoke that is easy and a burden that is light. For the strong version of 21-4-10 it is the same thing: **a burden that was chosen does not oppress**.

sections.h2: How to find the 21-4-10 tail from a date of birth
paragraphs: The 21-4-10 tail appears when the three numbers of a date of birth add up to 28, 37, 46 or 55: all of these sums reduce to 10. The calculation goes like this:

ol: A is the day of birth. If it is greater than 22, add its digits: 29 → 11, 31 → 4.
B is the number of the month.
C is the sum of the digits of the year; if it is greater than 22, add the digits again: 1986 → 24 → 6.
If A + B + C equals 28, 37, 46 or 55, the tail is 21-4-10.

paragraphs: Example: 15.07.1986. A = 15, B = 7, C = 6, sum 28. The rest follows on its own:

The Wheel at the root of this tail is never reached directly: the sum of the date always goes past 22 and is reduced. If the three numbers add up to exactly 10, the root is also The Wheel, but the tail is a different one — 3-13-10, with Judgement at the centre. A reduced ten gives a different centre: 38, 47, 56 and 65 all reduce to 11, and Strength becomes the centre.
This arithmetic leads to facts that are the same for everyone with 21-4-10:

ul: the centre of the chart is always Strength, and Manipura is always 11-11-22;
the relationship line always starts with The World;
the tail is possible on any day of the month and in any year since 1900: even 2000, the year with the fewest such dates, has nine;
it occurs most often in years whose year number is 21 — 1929, 1938, 1947, 1956, 1965, 1974, 1983, 1992: 41 dates in each;
the later the month, the more often the tail occurs: in December it is more than one and a half times as common as in January;
the sum 55 occurs on only 22 dates: 22 December in years whose number is 21, and 22 November or 21 December in years whose number is 22, for example 22.12.1983 or 21.12.1993.

paragraphs: How many such people are there? We went through every date from 1 January 1900 to 5 October 2026 — 46,299 days. The 21-4-10 tail comes from 3,957 of them, 8.55%: fifth place out of 26 possible tails, almost one person in twelve. Almost half of these dates come from the sum 28 (1,904), followed by 37 (1,516), 46 (515) and 55 (22). Generations differ: among people born in 1900–1959 the tail belongs to one in ten, in 1960–1999 to 8.4%, in 2000–2026 to 5.4%, about one in nineteen. But in all three generations it holds fifth place.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: The calculation follows the classic destiny matrix scheme: the tail is written as M–N–D, where D = A + B + C, the centre E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M, and sums over 22 are reduced by adding their digits. Frequencies come from running every date through the site's calculator.

Arthur Edward Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910; 1922 reprint): symbolism of the cards — Part II, divinatory meanings — Part III, history of the images and the views of Lévi and Christian on The World's garland — Part I. Quotations are from the original.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015), chapter 9: The World, The Emperor, The Wheel of Fortune, Strength. Quotations are from the original.

Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy (around 524): Book I, prose 5; Book II, proses 1–2; Book III, poem 2; Book IV, prose 6; Book V, prose 2. Quotations are our translation from the Latin; the biography follows widely available sources.
Carmina Burana, a thirteenth-century manuscript: the labels around the Wheel of Fortune.
Mikhail Lermontov, Mtsyri (1839). Alexander Pushkin, "It's time, my friend, it's time! The heart asks for peace…" (1834). The Gospel of Matthew, 11:30. Russian quotations are our translation.
The folk names of the tail and the legends about it follow common destiny matrix readings.
The link between the three positions, the comparisons with Boethius and Lermontov, and the practices are the author's interpretation. Waite and Wen do not describe the destiny matrix or karmic tails.

paragraphs: For a couple, 21-4-10 connects a broad horizon of wishes with the need to organise change. Here the World is the entry to the task, the Emperor, with the structure of daily life, is its middle, and the Wheel of Fortune is the main task: getting through changing circumstances together.

faq.q: Is it true that 21-4-10 is an "oppressed soul" who lived in captivity in a past life?
faq.a: There is no reason to think so. The legend of a past life under someone else's power — or, in another version, the life of a despot — cannot be verified in any way: numbers say nothing about past incarnations. The tail's cards describe not a biography but a mechanism: open space that is taken in hand and held so tightly that it becomes a weight. **The tail does not say who oppressed the person** — it shows where the person holds the key themselves.

faq.q: Who is the oppressor in the 21-4-10 tail — other people or the person themselves?
faq.a: The Emperor sits in the tail's mechanism, so both roles are inside: a person can live under someone else's throne, take the throne themselves, or be on the throne and under it at once, governing themselves more harshly than any boss. But the tail neither explains nor excuses real pressure from outside. If another person threatens, controls money and contacts, or uses force, this is not karma to work through but a reason to seek help: a local emergency number, crisis services, a psychologist.

faq.q: Why do I have 21-4-10 both as my karmic tail and on my relationship line?
faq.a: Both lines start at the same point M, so everyone with the tail has The World at the start of the relationship line. A full match of 21-4-10 on both lines happens when the year number is 5 or 14: the years 1904, 1913, 1922, 1931, 1940, 1949, 1958, 1967, 1976, 1985, 1994, 2003, 2012 and 2021. This is the case for 329 of the 3,957 dates, about one in twelve people with the tail. Then one scenario describes both the karmic loop and the way of building a couple, and it is most useful to work with it in relationships.

It shares its root, The Wheel of Fortune, with 3-13-10, but the two reach it by different paths. In 3-13-10 the date adds up to exactly 10, Judgement stands at the centre, The Empress at the entry and Death in the mechanism: there the loop runs on breaks and endings, not on walls. It shares its entry, The World, with 21-10-16 and 21-10-7, but in those tails The Wheel is the mechanism, and the root is The Tower or The Chariot. In 21-4-10 the mechanism is The Emperor with his walls, and The Wheel is the root task: learning stability in motion.

faq.q: Why is 21-4-10 more common in older generations?
faq.a: Because of the year number. The tail needs a large date sum — 28 or more — and in the last century the year number was usually a two-digit one, up to 22. After 2000 it became small, from 2 to 12, and the day and month have to make up almost the whole sum by themselves. So among people born in 1900–1959 the tail belongs to one in ten, while among those born in 2000–2026 it belongs to about one in nineteen. This is calendar arithmetic, not a sign of a special destiny for a generation.

faq.q: Does 21-4-10 mean emigration, prison or divorce?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events: not moves, not imprisonment, not divorces. The words "emigration" and "flight" in Waite's divinatory list for The World are an image of the mechanism: a pull towards open space that easily turns into escape. For one person the loop runs inside, in thoughts of a packed suitcase; for another, in changes of city and job; for a third, it is barely noticeable. **The calculation describes a possible scenario; it does not assign a fate.**

There is no ritual that cancels the tail, and the numbers of the date do not change. What changes is something else: the scenario stops switching on automatically. The signs are that rules get reviewed without a sense of disaster, change is no longer met with new walls, and leaving and coming back no longer feel like escape and surrender.

faq.q: What if a child has the 21-4-10 tail?
faq.a: Do not retell the "oppressed soul" legend to the child: a label easily becomes one more wall. It helps more to explain rules rather than simply impose them, to give the child a small territory of their own where they set the order, and not to shield them from every change. The reverse matters too: do not make the child the guard of someone else's order, a little "grown-up" making sure everything is as it should be. That way the tail's mechanism gets less to feed on from early childhood.

faq.q: Is the 21-4-10 tail different for women and men?
faq.a: No. Sex plays no part in the calculation and does not change the numbers, so the tail and its scenario are the same. Only the settings differ: where a person builds their fortress and whose authority weighs more for them. The moves themselves — open space, orb, weight, turn — do not depend on sex.

faq.q: Why is Strength number 11 at the centre here, when tarot books number Strength VIII?
faq.a: The destiny matrix uses the old Marseille numbering, where 8 is Justice and 11 is Strength. Waite swapped these cards in his deck and says so himself in his description of Strength, so in books based on his deck Strength is number VIII. The card's meaning does not change: it rests on the name and the image — a woman leading a lion on a chain of flowers.

intro: The cards are numbered as in the destiny matrix and the old Marseille deck: 11 is Strength. In Waite's deck this card is number VIII, but the meaning rests on the card's name, not on its number.

report: The card considered the best in the tarot deck opens a karmic loop called "The Oppressed Soul". The World is the first card of the 21-4-10 tail. After it come The Emperor and The Wheel of Fortune, and everyone with this tail has Strength at the centre of the chart.

The legends about the tail argue over the main point: who oppressed whom. In one version the soul spent its past life under someone else's will and got used to giving itself up. In the other it was that will: it laid down rigid rules and broke those who did not fit them. Neither version can be checked: numbers say nothing about past lives. But the name does not rest on the legend alone. It is written in the cards themselves — and in the Russian word: ugnetat, "to oppress", comes from gnesti, "to press down", and a gnyot is a weight placed on top to press something down.

report.h3: A chain harder to break than iron

report: Writing about the history of The World's image, Arthur Edward Waite notes that the garland around the dancing figure looks like a chain of flowers. According to one old reading, the garland should be made of roses, and this, in Éliphas Lévi's words, is the very chain that is **less easily broken than a chain of iron**. Waite's next sentence says that an iron crown may lie more lightly on the head than a crown of gold on kings.

One paragraph about the first card holds the whole tail. A chain of roses holds tighter than an iron one. A crown of gold weighs more than an iron one. And a crowned monarch is the tail's second card, The Emperor. The third is The Wheel of Fortune, and Benebell Wen, author of the textbook Holistic Tarot, opens her description of it with the words: "Key 10: Wheel of Fortune is the karma card." History repeats; the past becomes the future.
In 21-4-10 the weight on top is rarely made of iron. More often it is made of what a person values most: order, protection, permanence.

report.h3: A world taken in hand becomes an orb

report: The loop begins with open space. Something becomes a whole world — a person, a job, a city, a dream — and the urge is to have everything at once. So as not to lose it, the world is taken in hand. Waite's Emperor holds a globe in his left hand; in Russian this emblem of rule is called a derzhava, from derzhat, "to hold". Routine, rules, control, "let's make it safe". Waite's divinatory list for The Emperor includes "Stability, power, protection", and the walls really do protect. The trouble is that they cannot tell what they are protecting against — a storm or open space.

Next to The Emperor, Wen recalls King Midas, who "died of hunger, because all that he touched turned to gold and **gold cannot nourish**." That is how the tail's mechanism works. Love becomes a stone wall that is safe and cramped to live behind, work becomes golden handcuffs, a dream becomes a suitcase that stays packed in the head for years. When it gets cramped, the wheel turns: coldness, leaving, a move. And in the new place the world is taken in hand again, and the same fortress goes up.

Russian holds this mechanism in one word. Volya is the power to command, and volya is also freedom, the opposite of nevolya, "captivity". In 21-4-10 one volya builds walls while the other asks to be let out, and both belong to the same person. That is why each legend is half right: the oppressed and the oppressor here sit in different seats of one mechanism.

The loop's price is a life put off until "later", a well-ordered life with no air in it, and a cage that sooner or later gets built for loved ones too. If the sense of being trapped becomes unbearable, that is a reason to contact a psychologist, and in danger to call a local emergency number or crisis line. And if the pressure comes from another person — threats, control, violence — this is not a karmic scenario to work through but a situation that calls for help.

report.h3: The sphinx taken off the wheel

report: On Waite's wheel sits a sphinx — "the equilibrium therein". Sometimes, Waite writes, the sphinx is drawn on a separate pedestal above the wheel, and this defrauds the symbolism, because its essential idea is **stability amidst movement**. The 21-4-10 mechanism does exactly that: it takes the sphinx off the wheel and looks for stability in walls rather than in motion. And behind the image of the Wheel, Waite says, lies the denial of fatality, so "it's fate" is the least accurate explanation of this loop.

Fifteen hundred years ago a prisoner heard the same thing. Boethius, head of the court administration under King Theodoric, ended up in prison and there wrote The Consolation of Philosophy — the book that made Fortune's wheel one of the great images of the Middle Ages. Philosophy asks him whether he is really trying to hold back the rush of a turning wheel: "Most foolish of mortals, if it stops, it is no longer Fortune." And she explains that each thing is the freer from fate the nearer it comes to the pivot around which everything turns. Souls that help along their own slavery become "in a way, captives of their own freedom."

report.h3: The Wheel plus Strength make The World

report: This tail does have a pivot, and it is the same for everyone. The centre of the chart is always Strength: the entry point is the sum of the root and the centre, and The World comes out of The Wheel only together with Strength. The open space a person reaches for at the entry is made not of walls but of a turning that cannot be stopped and a strength that has no need to press down.

Strength has the same chain as The World. In Waite's description the woman has already tamed the lion, and it is led by a chain of flowers — "the sweet yoke and the light burden" of a law taken into the heart of hearts. The difference is not in the chain but in who put it on. Strength, for Wen, is mastery over one's own fears, not over people and circumstances. The stability The Emperor looks for in walls lies at the centre: in mastery over one's own fear of change.

So the way out is not escape — escape only moves the walls to a new place. It lies in testing every rule with the question "why", reviewing order before it sets hard, letting open space in a little at a time and regularly, and looking for what stays steady while everything moves. A sign that the loop has loosened: staying no longer means "giving in", and leaving no longer means "running away".

The strong version of 21-4-10 is a person who builds things that others are free inside: families where the rules are explained, teams where order serves the work. Waite's World figure dances inside the garland, under the guard of watchers — a dance inside the frame, not an escape from it. **A burden that was chosen does not oppress.**
